issues.legal_issue: A landholder challenging a land-reform acquisition law must show that the land is outside the constitutional category of estates to establish that the law does not apply to it.
material_facts: The petitions gave little information about the petitioners’ titles or why their lands were not estates.
The High Court had made categorical findings that the lands involved in the related proceedings were estates.
The State asserted that the petitioners’ lands were estates.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners had not shown prima facie that their lands were not estates, and the Court could not hold that they were unaffected by the amended land-reform law.
issues.legal_principle: The Court placed on the petitioners the burden of establishing that their lands were not estates within Article 31A(2), particularly in light of the High Court’s findings and the absence of supporting material in the petitions. It also relied on U.P. State v. Raja Anand for the distinction between land held as part of an agricultural estate and land held independently.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: The landholders brought a constitutional challenge to a law providing for acquisition and redistribution of land.
predicates.petitioners_provided_no_evidence_that_la: The landholders did not provide material showing that their land fell outside the relevant category of estates.
predicates.prior_court_found_land_was_an_estate: A prior court had found that the land involved was an estate.

issues.definition: When landholders challenge an acquisition law but provide no evidence that their land is outside the relevant estate category despite a prior finding that it is an estate, they fail to show that the law does not apply to their land.

issues.legal_issue: A law included in the constitutional schedule with the specified protection cannot be challenged under the constitutional property-right provisions identified by the Court.
material_facts: The original land-reform Act had been included in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution.
The amending Act was not included in that Schedule and could claim protection only under Article 31A.
issues.conclusion: The original Act could not be challenged under Article 31 because of its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B protected the original Act after its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule. The Court distinguished that Act from the later amending Act, which was not included there and therefore had to rely on Article 31A for protection.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant brought a constitutional challenge to a land-reform law.
predicates.challenged_law_was_included_in_protected: The challenged law had been included in a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from the specified constitutional challenge.

issues.definition: A challenge under the specified property-right provisions is barred when the challenged land-reform law is included in a constitutionally protected schedule.

issues.legal_issue: Lowering a ceiling under a later law does not require market-value compensation for the difference from the ceiling under an earlier law.
material_facts: The earlier Act fixed a ceiling that was higher than the ceiling fixed by the amending Act.
The petitioners argued that the reduction required compensation at market value for the difference between the two ceilings.
issues.conclusion: The reduction of the ceiling did not attract the second proviso to Article 31A(1), and compensation for the difference between the earlier and later ceilings was not required.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the phrase “ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force” in the second proviso to Article 31A(1) as referring to the ceiling imposed by the law fixing the applicable limit, not an earlier law that had been amended or repealed.

predicates.challenge_to_reduced_land_ceiling: A landholder challenged a lower ceiling imposed by a later land-reform law.
predicates.later_law_replaced_earlier_ceiling: A later law replaced the ceiling imposed by an earlier law.
predicates.compensation_claim_rests_on_difference_b: The landholder sought compensation on the ground that the later ceiling was lower than the earlier ceiling.

issues.definition: When a later law replaces an earlier land ceiling and the compensation claim rests on the difference between them, compensation for that difference is not required.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature may bring incorporated landholders within a land ceiling even if an earlier law did not impose that ceiling on them.
material_facts: The earlier Act did not apply its ceiling to companies or other incorporated bodies.
The amending Act imposed a ceiling on all persons, including incorporated bodies.
The companies challenged their inclusion under the amended ceiling scheme.
issues.conclusion: The legislature could prescribe a ceiling for incorporated and unincorporated landholders, and the earlier Act’s exclusion of incorporated bodies did not prevent their inclusion by the amending Act.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a legislature may extend a land ceiling to incorporated bodies even where an earlier law had not covered them.

predicates.challenge_to_land_ceiling: A landholder challenged the application of a land ceiling.
predicates.earlier_law_excluded_incorporated_holder: An earlier law did not impose the relevant ceiling on incorporated landholders.
predicates.later_law_applies_ceiling_to_all_holders: A later law imposes the ceiling on incorporated and unincorporated landholders.

issues.definition: A later law may apply a land ceiling to incorporated landholders even though an earlier law excluded them.

issues.legal_issue: A broad power to reserve acquired land for public purposes must be confined to public purposes that advance agrarian reform to receive constitutional protection as an agrarian-reform measure.
material_facts: The provision authorized reservation of land vested in the government for any public purpose.
The provision’s language could cover purposes unrelated to agrarian reform.
A prior High Court interpretation had confined the corresponding reservation power to purposes connected with agrarian reform.
issues.conclusion: The provision was read down to permit reservation only for public purposes that bring about agrarian reform; it was not struck down altogether.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule of construction recognized in Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab and read the provision consistently with Article 31A. Acquisition for a public purpose unrelated to agrarian reform could not receive Article 31A protection.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant brought a constitutional challenge to a land-reform law’s power to reserve acquired land.
predicates.reservation_language_covers_public_purpo: The reservation language is broad enough to cover public purposes unrelated to agrarian reform.

issues.definition: When a challenged reservation power covers purposes beyond agrarian reform, it is confined to purposes that advance agrarian reform.

issues.legal_issue: Measures granting permanent rights to agricultural-land hut occupants and settling them on small holdings in panchayat areas can form part of agrarian reform.
material_facts: The challenged provisions protected kudikidappukars from eviction and enabled them to obtain rights in their homesteads and adjoining land.
The State’s evidence described kudikidappukars as people who had historically lived on land in return for services, often including agricultural labour.
The provisions concerned lands in panchayat areas.
issues.conclusion: The settlement of kudikidappukars and tenants of kudiyiruppus on small holdings in panchayat areas was covered by agrarian reform or purposes ancillary to it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the problem of kudikidappukars was intimately connected with agricultural land and that improving their circumstances and granting permanent rights could fall within agrarian reform under Article 31A. It referred to Armugha Konar v. Sanku Muthammal, Saimva Umma v. Kunhammad, and Mariam v. Ouseph Xavier, as well as the history of protective legislation described by the State. The Court confined this holding to panchayat areas and did not decide the corresponding problem in municipal areas.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant brought a constitutional challenge to a measure reallocating rights in land.
predicates.occupants_live_on_agricultural_land_in_p: The occupants whose rights are affected live on agricultural land in a panchayat area.
predicates.occupants_have_historical_or_work_relate: The occupants have a historical or work-related connection to the land, including residence there in connection with agricultural labour.

issues.definition: A measure settling occupants with a historical or work-related connection to agricultural land in a panchayat area can qualify as agrarian reform.

issues.legal_issue: A compulsory purchase right allowing a hut occupant to acquire land for less than market value may offend the constitutional restriction on acquisition of certain land within the owner’s ceiling and personal cultivation.
material_facts: The purchase provision allowed a kudikidappukaran to purchase the land occupied by the homestead for consideration below market value.
The Court identified the relevant situation as land below the ceiling area and within the landlord’s personal cultivation.
issues.conclusion: In that identified situation, the purchase provision would be hit by the second proviso to Article 31A.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Article 31A restricts the protection available for acquisition of land within the specified ceiling and personal-cultivation conditions unless the required compensation safeguard is met.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_l: A litigant brought a constitutional challenge to a law requiring land to be transferred to an occupant.
predicates.occupant_may_purchase_below_market_value: The law permits the occupant to purchase the land for less than its market value.
predicates.land_is_within_owner_ceiling_and_persona: The land is within the owner’s ceiling and is under the owner’s personal cultivation.

issues.definition: A below-market compulsory purchase provision lacks the relevant constitutional protection when it concerns land within the owner’s ceiling and personal cultivation.

issues.legal_issue: The withdrawal of exemptions for pepper and arecanut plantations does not violate equality when the affected lands are estates within the constitutional definition.
material_facts: The amending law removed exemptions that had applied to certain pepper and arecanut gardens.
The petitioners relied on the earlier decision concerning unequal treatment of plantations.

The Court accepted the State’s position that pepper and arecanut were mainly homestead-garden crops and that the materials did not establish a basis for treating them like tea, coffee, or rubber plantations.
The Court’s conclusion was conditional on the lands being estates.
issues.conclusion: The withdrawal of protection for pepper and arecanut plantations could not be challenged under Article 14 if the lands were estates within Article 31A(2)(a).
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Karimbil Kunhikoman v. State of Kerala, in which the earlier law’s treatment of plantations had been held discriminatory in relation to lands not protected as estates. For estate lands, Article 31A(2)(a) prevented the equality challenge described here.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge_to_lan: A landholder brought an equality-based constitutional challenge to a land-reform law.
predicates.land_is_an_estate: The affected land falls within the constitutional category of estates.
predicates.law_withdraws_special_exemption_from_pep: The challenged law removes a special exemption that had applied to pepper or arecanut land.

issues.definition: An equality challenge to removal of a pepper or arecanut exemption is rejected when the affected land is an estate.

issues.legal_issue: The treatment of cashew and coconut gardens under the land-reform law is not discriminatory on the grounds advanced in this case.
material_facts: The petitioners argued that cashew and coconut gardens should receive the same protection as plantations of tea, coffee, rubber, and other crops.
The State maintained that these crops were not cultivated in the same manner as the protected plantation crops and were generally grown on smaller holdings.
The Court found no basis in the materials before it to reject the State’s position.
issues.conclusion: The Act was not discriminatory with regard to cashew and coconut gardens.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the distinction under Article 14 and accepted the State’s explanation of the different cultivation patterns and the State’s view of its agricultural economy. It distinguished the circumstances addressed in Karimbil Kunhikoman v. State of Kerala.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge_to_lan: A landholder brought an equality-based constitutional challenge to a land-reform law.
predicates.law_treats_cashew_or_coconut_gardens_dif: The law treats cashew or coconut gardens differently from other plantations.
predicates.cultivation_patterns_are_materially_diff: The crops are cultivated in patterns materially different from those of the plantations receiving different treatment.

issues.definition: Different treatment of cashew or coconut gardens is not discriminatory when their cultivation patterns materially differ from those of other plantations.

issues.legal_issue: The removal of an exemption for land adjoining a rubber plantation does not conflict with legislation regulating the rubber industry when that legislation does not require expansion of the plantation.
material_facts: The amending law withdrew an exemption for land contiguous to rubber plantations.
The petitioners argued that federal legislation regulating the rubber industry prevented acquisition of land reserved for possible plantation expansion.
The legislation required a licence to plant or replant rubber and assigned the Rubber Board a role in developing the industry, but did not require owners to bring additional land under rubber.
issues.conclusion: The withdrawal of the exemption for land contiguous to rubber plantations could not be challenged on the grounds advanced.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh and State of Maharashtra v. Patilchand, the Court distinguished regulation of an industry and its manufacturing process from regulation of the supply of raw material or land use. It held that the rubber legislation did not authorize or require expansion of plantations and did not prevent the State’s land-reform measure.

predicates.challenge_to_land_reform_law_based_on_in: A landholder challenged a land-reform law on the ground that it conflicted with legislation regulating an industry.
predicates.land_is_adjoining_industrial_plantation: The land at issue adjoins a plantation used to supply an industrial raw material.
predicates.industry_law_does_not_require_expansion_: The industry legislation does not require the owner to expand the plantation onto the adjoining land.

issues.definition: Removal of an adjoining-land exemption is valid when industry legislation does not require plantation expansion onto that land.

issues.legal_issue: Land interspersed among commercial undertaking sites or surrounding residential sites in municipalities is not agricultural land fit for acquisition under an agrarian-reform law.
material_facts: The law could reach land interspersed among sites of commercial undertakings and land surrounding house sites in municipalities.
The Court found that such land could not be treated as agricultural merely because it was within the law’s general scope or could potentially be cultivated.
The statutory exemptions did not ensure that all such non-agricultural land would be excluded.
issues.conclusion: The Act could not acquire such interspersed land because it was not agricultural land fit for acquisition under the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A protects acquisition for agrarian reform, not acquisition of non-agricultural land merely for redistribution. The Court rejected the State’s broad assertion that lands remained agricultural unless altered by construction, and considered the actual character and situation of the land.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant brought a constitutional challenge to acquisition under a land-reform law.
predicates.land_is_interspersed_among_commercial_si: The land lies among commercial undertaking sites or surrounds residential sites in a municipality.
predicates.land_is_not_agricultural: The land is not agricultural land fit for acquisition as part of agrarian reform.

issues.definition: Land among commercial sites or around municipal homes cannot be acquired under an agrarian-reform law when it is not agricultural land.

issues.legal_issue: A jungle or forest is not an estate merely by being included in a holding, but it may fall within an estate when held as part of land used for agriculture or an ancillary purpose.
material_facts: Some petitioners held forest and jungle land.
The Court distinguished land held independently as jungle from forest land included in an estate consisting of land held for agricultural purposes or purposes ancillary to agriculture.
Private forests were specially exempted from acquisition under the Act.
issues.conclusion: A holding consisting only of jungle could not be acquired as an estate on that basis; forest or jungle land included within an agricultural estate could fall within the estate, subject to the statutory exemption for private forests.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 31A(2)(a) and (iii) and relied on U.P. State v. Raja Anand, which held that forest or waste land is not an estate under the relevant category unless held or let for agricultural purposes or purposes ancillary to them. The Court also noted the Act’s special exemption for private forests.

rule.if: land_reform_acquisition_case and land_is_forest_or_jungle and (holding_contains_only_forest_or_jungle or not land_is_part_of_agricultural_estate)

predicates.land_reform_acquisition_case: The dispute concerns acquisition under a land-reform law.
predicates.land_is_forest_or_jungle: The land is forest or jungle land.
predicates.holding_contains_only_forest_or_jungle: The holding or tenure consists only of forest or jungle.
predicates.land_is_part_of_agricultural_estate: The forest or jungle land is held as part of an estate used for agriculture or an ancillary purpose.

issues.definition: Forest or jungle land is not acquirable as part of an agricultural estate when the holding consists only of it or it is not part of such an estate.

issues.legal_issue: A dairy farm that forms part of an estate is not exempt from acquisition solely because it is a dairy farm.
material_facts: A petitioner held land used as a dairy farm together with other lands.
The Court stated that dairy farms forming parts of estates were not exempt from the Act.
issues.conclusion: Dairy farms forming part of estates were not exempt from the Act.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the issue as one of whether the land formed part of an estate and found no basis for an exemption for a dairy farm that was part of that estate.

predicates.land_reform_acquisition_case: The dispute concerns acquisition under a land-reform law.
predicates.dairy_land_is_part_of_estate: The land used as a dairy farm forms part of an estate.

issues.definition: Dairy land forming part of an estate is not exempt merely because it is used as a dairy farm.

issues.legal_issue: Teak or eucalyptus land resulting from agricultural operations is agricultural land, while land covered by those trees growing spontaneously as forest or jungle is outside acquisition under the Act.
material_facts: Petitioners held land planted with teak or eucalyptus.
The Court distinguished trees resulting from agricultural operations from trees growing spontaneously in a jungle or forest.
issues.conclusion: Land planted with teak or eucalyptus through agricultural operations was agricultural land; land covered by spontaneously growing teak or eucalyptus was outside the purview of acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court classified the land according to how the trees came to be there: agricultural operations made the land agricultural, whereas spontaneous forest or jungle growth did not bring it within the acquisition provisions.

rule.if: land_reform_acquisition_case and land_is_covered_by_teak_or_eucalyptus and (trees_result_from_agricultural_operations or trees_grow_spontaneously_as_forest)

predicates.land_reform_acquisition_case: The dispute concerns acquisition under a land-reform law.
predicates.land_is_covered_by_teak_or_eucalyptus: The land is covered by teak or eucalyptus trees.
predicates.trees_result_from_agricultural_operation: The trees were planted or raised through agricultural operations.
predicates.trees_grow_spontaneously_as_forest: The trees grew spontaneously as part of a jungle or forest.

issues.definition: Teak or eucalyptus land is agricultural when the trees result from agricultural operations, but spontaneous forest growth is outside acquisition.
